title: How to Remove Sticky Grease From Kitchen Cabinets Easily
hook: Sticky, yellowish film on your kitchen cabinets, especially above the stove and around the handles. It attracts dust, and gets worse every month. In seven steps, you'll learn how to dissolve it with gentle products, with no harsh scrubbing and no damage to the finish. It's easier than it looks.
intro: Cabinet grease is a mix of cooking oil vapor, steam and dust that sticks to every surface in your kitchen. Because it builds up slowly, you may not notice until you touch it. The trick is to use a degreaser that breaks the oil down, rather than scrubbing hard, which can wear the finish. We'll start with the mildest option, and move up only if needed. First, a quick note. Always test any cleaner in a hidden spot. The whole job is gentle rather than heavy, so put on some music and take it one door at a time. You will be surprised how different the kitchen looks afterwards.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. Warm water and a good grease-cutting dish soap. Baking soda for stubborn areas. Soft microfiber cloths, at least three. An old, soft toothbrush for corners and carved edges. And white vinegar, but only for sealed or painted cabinets. You do not need steel wool, abrasive sponges or harsh oven cleaners. Most of these things are probably under your sink already, and none of them are expensive.
heroImagePrompt: Clean white kitchen cabinets with a hand wiping a door using a yellow microfiber cloth, bright morning light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Empty the area and test
steps.narration: Step one. Clear the counter below the cabinets and lay down a towel to catch drips. Find out what the cabinet finish is: sealed wood, painted wood, laminate or thermofoil. Then test your cleaning mix on a hidden spot, such as the inside of a door or the bottom edge, and wait a few minutes. If there's no discoloration or softening, you're good to go. Raw or unfinished wood needs much less moisture than other finishes. If you're unsure about the finish, ask the manufacturer or use only mild soap and water. Gloves help keep your hands soft.
steps.tip: Test in a hidden spot first
steps.mistake: Skipping the patch test on painted cabinets
steps.imagePrompt: A kitchen counter covered with a towel beneath wooden cabinets, ready for cleaning, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Dust and dry wipe first
steps.narration: Step two. Before you add any liquid, wipe the cabinets with a dry microfiber cloth to remove loose dust, lint and crumbs. Grease and dust together form a sticky paste, which becomes harder to clean once it's wet and smeared around. Work from the top down, and pay attention to the tops of cabinet doors, the corners and the area around the handles. A vacuum with a brush attachment is helpful for carved or ridged doors. Don't skip this, since wiping a dusty surface with a wet cloth turns the dirt into a grey smear.
steps.tip: Dry wipe from the top down
steps.imagePrompt: A hand dusting kitchen cabinet doors with a dry microfiber cloth, soft daylight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Mix a gentle degreaser
steps.narration: Step three. Fill a bowl or bucket with warm water, and add a few drops of grease-cutting dish soap. Stir it gently until it's slightly sudsy. This simple mix dissolves cooking oil on most finishes. For sealed or painted cabinets with heavy buildup, you can use a half and half mix of white vinegar and warm water instead. Avoid vinegar on unfinished wood, natural stone countertops and any glue seams. Never combine different cleaning products, and never use bleach. Prepare a fresh batch if the water turns cloudy. Warm water works much better than cold water on cooking oil.
steps.tip: Dish soap is the safest start
steps.imagePrompt: A bowl of warm soapy water with a microfiber cloth beside it on a kitchen counter, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Wipe and let it work
steps.narration: Step four. Dip a microfiber cloth in the solution and wring it out well, so it's damp but not dripping. Wipe a small section of the cabinet, and then let the solution sit for a minute or two. This dwell time lets the soap soften the grease, so you don't need to scrub. Rinse the cloth often, as it picks up oil. Work in small sections, using gentle circles, and move from the top of the cabinet to the bottom. Use a second cloth to rinse and wring it out regularly. It is better to take more passes than to use more liquid.
steps.imagePrompt: A damp yellow microfiber cloth wiping a greasy cabinet door, showing a clean streak, close-up, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Treat thick buildup
steps.narration: Step five. For stubborn, thick grease, mix baking soda with a little water to make a soft paste. Spread it on the sticky areas, let it sit for five minutes, and gently work it with the soft toothbrush, in small circles. Baking soda is mildly abrasive, so use light pressure, and avoid it on high-gloss finishes, which can dull. Pay attention to the handles, hinges and the grooves of paneled doors. Wipe the paste away with a clean damp cloth. Go slowly near hinges and edges, where the finish is thinnest. A pea-sized amount of paste goes a long way.
steps.tip: Soft toothbrush for grooves and handles
steps.mistake: Using abrasive scrubbers on cabinet doors
steps.imagePrompt: A soft toothbrush with white baking soda paste cleaning a cabinet handle area, macro, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Rinse and dry thoroughly
steps.narration: Step six. Go over every surface with a second cloth, dampened with plain water, to remove soap and any leftover grease. Soap residue can attract new dirt. Then immediately dry the cabinets with a dry microfiber cloth. Moisture left on wood can cause swelling or stains, especially near the edges and joints. Check the cabinets in the light from a few angles. If you see sticky patches, repeat the previous step on just those spots. A quick pass with a clean dry cloth also removes streaks, and leaves the surface smooth to the touch.
steps.mistake: Leaving water sitting on the surface
steps.imagePrompt: A hand drying a clean cabinet door with a dry white cloth, shiny finish, bright kitchen, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Stop grease building up again
steps.narration: Step seven. Prevention takes far less effort than cleaning. Use your extractor fan or range hood whenever you cook, and clean its filters monthly. Wipe the cabinets above the stove and around handles every week with a damp cloth. Cover pans while frying to cut down on spatter. If your cabinets have a new buildup layer, you'll remove it much faster. Keep a cloth near the stove, and wipe splashes on the day they happen. Wash the filters of your range hood in hot soapy water once a month, since clogged filters push grease into the room.
steps.tip: A weekly wipe takes two minutes
steps.mistake: Cooking without turning on the extractor fan
steps.imagePrompt: A kitchen range hood switched on above a stove with a pan cooking, clean cabinets beside it, photorealistic, no text

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, using too much water on wood. It can swell, warp or stain the surface, so keep the cloth damp, not wet. Second, scrubbing hard with abrasive pads, which scratch the finish and make future grease stick even more. And third, using harsh chemicals without testing. Some cleaners strip paint or varnish. Be gentle, test first, and let the soap do the work. A little patience beats a lot of scrubbing every time.

recap.narration: Let's recap. Clear the area and test in a hidden spot. Dust and dry wipe first. Mix a gentle degreaser. Wipe and let it work. Treat thick buildup with baking soda. Rinse and dry thoroughly. And stop the grease from coming back with a weekly wipe. Seven steps, about an hour, and kitchen cabinets that feel clean again. Gentle products, a little time, and dry cloths do all the work.

outro: That's how you remove sticky grease from kitchen cabinets. If your cabinets look brighter, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments which cabinet was the stickiest, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. Don't forget to give the handles a wipe before you go.

metadata.title: How to Remove Sticky Grease From Kitchen Cabinets Easily
metadata.description:
Sticky, greasy kitchen cabinets? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to remove sticky grease from kitchen cabinets with no harsh scrubbing: test the finish, dry wipe the dust, mix a gentle dish soap degreaser, let it work, treat thick buildup with baking soda, rinse and dry, and stop the grease from returning. Safe for most sealed or painted wood, laminate and thermofoil cabinets.

You'll need: warm water and dish soap, baking soda, soft microfiber cloths, an old soft toothbrush, white vinegar (optional).
